analysis.one_liner: Requires immigration authorities to use supervision programs instead of detention for vulnerable immigrants and parents.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its immigration subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to run supervision programs — community-based monitoring, case management, and support services — as an alternative to locking people up in immigration detention. It would bar detention outright for certain groups: asylum seekers, pregnant or nursing women, crime victims, trafficking victims, LGBTQ individuals, people with disabilities, parents of children under 18, and family caregivers. It would also create a coordinator inside DHS responsible for reuniting parents with children separated at or near the border, a direct response to the family separation practices of 2018.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants facing deportation who fall into vulnerable categories — asylum seekers, torture and trafficking victims, pregnant and nursing women, children and adults over 60, LGBTQ individuals, crime victims and witnesses, people with mental illness or disabilities — as well as parents and caregivers of children and dependents. Their families, including U.S.-citizen children who would otherwise lose a parent to detention, also benefit. Community-based nonprofits that provide supervision and case management services would gain contracts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Vulnerable immigrants, their children, and community nonprofits

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires DHS to establish a continuum of alternatives to detention, including community-based supervision and community support programs, and allows contracts with nongovernmental community organizations for case management and appearance assistance [S3].

Within 48 hours of taking someone into custody, DHS or an immigration judge must determine whether that person can be placed in an alternative program, and members of a vulnerable population, parents of children under 18, and caregivers may not be detained at all — they must go into community-based supervision [S3].

The bill defines 'vulnerable population' broadly to include asylum seekers, torture and trafficking victims, pregnant or nursing women, people under 21 or over 60, LGBTQ individuals, crime victims and witnesses, people with mental disorders or physical disabilities, and survivors of severe trauma or gender-based violence [S3].

It creates a Coordinator of Alternatives to Detention and Family Reunification inside DHS, appointed by and reporting to the Secretary, whose mission includes reunifying parents with children separated at or near a port of entry or within 100 miles of the border, with a report to Congress within 30 days [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the bill would shift spending away from immigration detention beds toward supervision contracts with community organizations, paid for by federal appropriations. For-profit detention companies and the agencies that fill detention beds would lose that revenue. Critics of supervision programs also argue taxpayers bear the cost of monitoring people who might otherwise be more quickly removed, and opponents of relaxed enforcement argued some individuals would fail to appear for proceedings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private detention contractors and DHS detention budgets

drawbacks.text: The bill makes non-detention mandatory for very broad categories — any parent of a child under 18, anyone over 60 or under 21, anyone self-reporting severe trauma — so opponents would argue it sharply limits the government's ability to detain people pending removal, and the text does not fund the new programs; its spending is 'subject to the availability of appropriations' [S3].

The bill creates a new presidentially appointed coordinator position inside DHS and obligates every executive department to respond promptly to the coordinator's requests, which raises questions about layered bureaucracy and authority over immigration enforcement; the coordinator position itself sunsets after three years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: supervision programs generally cost far less per person than detention and keep families intact, while detention is the more restrictive and expensive option. The bill's mandatory categories are drawn so broadly that the cost and enforcement effects would depend heavily on how DHS implemented supervision, and the bill provides no dedicated funding. For the people it covers — parents of U.S. citizen children, asylum seekers, torture survivors — the human stakes of avoiding detention are large; the fiscal cost is a shift within the immigration enforcement budget rather than a new large expense.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late August 2018, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its immigration subcommittee, and no markup, vote, or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Anthony Brown of Maryland introduced the bill on August 31, 2018, joined by Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].

On October 9, 2018, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Border Security, where it remained; the complete action history shows no further action, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
The bill drew 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of the bill's action ever progressed past subcommittee referral before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The immigration detention industry and the status quo: detention contractors and the agencies relying on detention beds kept their revenue, and vulnerable immigrants and separated families received no new protections, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Detention industry and the enforcement status quo

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and then to the immigration subcommittee and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no floor consideration — during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill received no Republican support; it also never advanced past subcommittee referral in a Republican-led committee [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would require community supervision instead of detention for large categories of immigrants, shrinking the detention population that companies operating detention facilities are paid to hold. For the affected individuals and their families, that shift is a gain; for the industry, it is lost revenue.

The bill allows DHS to contract with nongovernmental community organizations for case management, appearance assistance, and screenings, creating funding for providers of supervision and support services. Their service of keeping people out of detention and attending hearings runs alongside the interests of the people served.
